Peace elsewhere does not answer Jerusalem's distress

The patrol reports in verse 11 that the whole earth is at rest. That sounds like good news. For Jerusalem it is not. The world is calm while the city still lies in ruins. In verse 12 an angel asks God, “how long?” Verse 15 says God is angry with the nations at ease. They went further in harming Judah than he intended.
The measured city receives a promise larger than its walls

The man in verse 1 means to measure the city, perhaps for its walls. Verse 4 says the city will be too full for walls. Verse 5 gives a different protection: God himself as a wall of fire. Verse 11 then widens who lives inside. Many nations will join the LORD. He calls them “my people,” the name once given to Israel alone. The promise is larger than any line can mark.
Changed clothing answers the accusation against the priest

Verse 3 admits that Joshua’s clothes are filthy. The accuser has grounds. The reply in verse 2 does not claim Joshua is clean. It points to God’s choice of Jerusalem. Verse 4 then removes the clothes and the guilt together. Joshua does not change his own garments. Verse 7 gives him duties after the gift, not before it.
The vision directs attention back to unfinished work

The vision is strange, and its message is practical. The temple’s foundation was laid, and then the work stalled (Ezra 4:24). Verse 6 says how it will be finished. The builders have no army or great strength. God’s Spirit will do it. Verse 9 promises that the hands that began will finish. Verse 10 speaks to those who scorned a small beginning.
Wrongdoing leaves houses without their supposed protection

The scroll names two wrongs: theft and false oaths. One harms a neighbor, and the other misuses God’s name. Verse 4 says the curse goes into the offender’s house. A house is where people keep what they took and feel safe. The curse stays there and takes the building apart. So wrongdoing removes its own shelter. The second vision carries wickedness out of the land altogether.
A crown links distant gifts with the temple's future

The crown is set on a priest, not on the governor. Verse 13 then describes one figure called the Branch. He builds the temple, sits on a throne, and serves as priest. Israel had kept those two offices apart. Here there is “counsel of peace” between them. The gold comes from exiles who just arrived (verse 10). Verse 15 says more people from far away will share in the building.
A question about fasting becomes a question about injured neighbors

The fifth-month fast mourned the burning of the temple (2 Kings 25:8–9). God does not answer the question until 8:19. He first asks whom the fasting served (verses 5–6). Then verses 9–10 repeat the earlier prophets’ demand. Four groups are named: widows, orphans, foreigners, and the poor. Neglect of them led to the loss now being mourned. Grief over the loss means little if its cause continues.
A restored city must be safe enough for ordinary life

Verses 4–5 measure the restored city by two groups. Old people sit outside, and children play in the streets. These are the ages least able to defend themselves. No walls or soldiers are mentioned. A city is safe when they can use its streets. Verses 16–17 say what that takes: true speech and fair courts. Verse 19 finally answers the question about fasting from chapter 7.
The promised king removes weapons while the chapter still contains battle

Verse 9 brings the king on a donkey, not a war horse. Verse 10 then says what he removes. The chariots of Ephraim and the horses of Jerusalem are Israel’s own. He disarms his own side. His rule spreads by speaking peace. Verses 13–15 still describe battle, and the chapter keeps both pictures. Matthew 21:5 quotes verse 9 about Jesus entering Jerusalem.
Failed guidance leaves people scattered like an untended flock

Verse 1 says to ask the LORD, who makes the storm clouds. Verse 2 names where the people have been asking. They turn to household idols, diviners, and dreamers. The comfort they receive is false. The verse then states a result in society. People drift like sheep and suffer because no one leads them. In verse 3 God answers by becoming their shepherd himself.
Selling the flock turns care into profit

Verse 5 names three groups who gain from the flock. Buyers slaughter and go unpunished. Sellers say, “Blessed be the LORD, for I am rich.” The flock’s own shepherds feel no pity. Religious words cover the trade. The good shepherd’s pay in verse 12 is thirty pieces of silver. Exodus 21:32 sets that as the price of a slave.
Rescue outside the city comes before the city's honor

Verse 7 sets an order for the rescue. The “tents of Judah,” the countryside, are saved first. The verse gives the reason. The capital and the royal house must not rise above the others. Verse 10 then turns victory into mourning. The leading families weep one by one (verses 12–14). John 19:37 applies verse 10 to the death of Jesus.
Cleansing includes the collapse of false claims and the testing of survivors

The chapter moves in four steps. A fountain cleanses (verse 1), and false prophecy ends (verses 2–6). The shepherd is struck (verse 7), and the survivors are refined (verses 8–9). Being among the survivors is not the end. Fire tests them as silver and gold are tested. Verse 9 closes with both sides speaking. God says, “It is my people,” and they say, “The LORD is my God.”
Holiness reaches ordinary pots after a vision of terrible conflict

The chapter begins with a city plundered (verse 2). It ends with kitchens. “Holy to the LORD” was engraved on the high priest’s gold plate (Exodus 28:36). Verse 20 puts those words on horses’ bells. Verse 21 makes every pot in the city fit for sacred use. The line between holy and common is removed by raising everything. Verse 16 includes survivors from the nations in the worship.
